per100gNote: All values are per 100 g of the edible portion, as purchased/raw unless the name says otherwise. Values are rounded from USDA FoodData Central (Foundation Foods, SR Legacy, and FNDDS), which is public domain. See docs/DATA-SOURCES.md.
unitsNote: units maps a recipe unit to grams of that ingredient. 'each' is one medium item. Cup measures are for the prep state named in the recipe.
gardenZone: Garden notes are written for USDA hardiness zone 6a (last frost around May 10-15, first frost around October 10-15). Shift by about two weeks per zone.

garden.harvest: Mid-July when the lower third of leaves brown
garden.note: The single highest-value thing to grow in Ohio: plant once in fall, ignore it all winter, harvest a year of garlic.

garden.harvest: 70 days; fall carrots after frost are sweeter

garden.harvest: August–September; leave green peppers on the plant to turn red

garden.harvest: Spring and fall; side shoots keep coming after the main head

garden.sow: Transplant August 1 for a fall crop

garden.note: Two plants feed a family of four and half the neighborhood. Pick at 6-8 inches.

garden.harvest: October; cures and stores until February in a cool room

garden.sow: Direct sow after May 20, again in early July
garden.harvest: 55 days; pick every other day or they get tough

garden.sow: Plant crowns April, first real harvest in year three

garden.harvest: After the first hard frost in November

garden.sow: Direct sow April 1 (St. Patrick's Day planting works here)
Direct sow July 1 for a fall bulb crop
Direct sow April and again August
garden.harvest: 55 days; the greens are as good as chard

items.name: Lemon
items.tips: Acid is the single best substitute for salt. When a dish tastes flat, it usually needs lemon, not more salt.

garden.note: Northeast Ohio is orchard country — Patterson Fruit Farm and Szalay's are closer than a spray schedule is worth.

garden.sow: Plant bushes in spring, acidify the soil
garden.note: Ohio soil runs alkaline; blueberries need pH 4.5-5.5, so plant them in a dedicated bed with peat and pine bark.

items.name: Fresh ginger

subs.note: Ground ginger is warmer and less bright. It works in a braise or a bake, not in a dressing.

items.tips: Freeze the knob whole and grate it frozen on a microplane — no peeling, no waste.

garden.harvest: Bolts fast in heat — succession sowing is the only way

items.name: Flat-leaf parsley
items.tips: A handful of chopped parsley over anything is the cheapest way to make home food look plated.

subs.note: Dried basil is for cooking into a sauce, not for finishing — add it early and it has time to open up.

garden.note: Pinch the flower tips weekly and one plant supplies pesto all summer. Grows happily in a pot by the back door.

garden.sow: Plant in a pot, never in the ground
garden.note: Mint will colonize a garden bed in two seasons. Container only.

garden.sow: Direct sow April, self-seeds forever after

subs.note: Thyme is milder and less resinous than rosemary — a fair swap in a braise, less so where rosemary is the point.

garden.harvest: Year-round if you bring the pot indoors — it will not survive an Ohio winter outside

subs.note: Dried thyme is more concentrated than fresh, so this is about a third of the volume. Add it early rather than at the end.

garden.harvest: Perennial here — survives zone 6 winters and comes back every year

items.name: Eggs (large)

subs.note: Crumble it and press out the water first. It scrambles, but it will not set or bind.

items.heartNote: Current AHA guidance treats one egg a day as fine for most healthy adults; for someone managing existing heart disease, keeping whole eggs to about 4 a week and using extra whites is the common recommendation.

items.name: Plain nonfat Greek yogurt
items.tips: Replaces sour cream and mayo one-for-one and adds 10 g of protein per half cup.

items.name: Unsweetened soy milk
items.heartNote: Soy is the only common plant milk with protein comparable to dairy, and FDA allows a qualified heart-health claim for soy protein.

items.name: Parmesan cheese

subs.note: Savory and cheesy, but it will not melt or brown. Use it as a finish, not inside a bake.

items.heartNote: Very high sodium and saturated fat, but you only need a tablespoon or two — used as a finisher, not a filler.
items.dietNote: True Parmigiano-Reggiano uses animal rennet. For a strict vegetarian, buy a domestic parmesan labeled vegetarian, or use nutritional yeast.

items.name: Feta cheese
items.tips: Buy the block in brine, not pre-crumbled — better texture, and it lasts a month.

items.name: Sharp cheddar
items.heartNote: Sharp cheddar delivers more flavor per gram than mild, so you can use a third less for the same effect.

items.name: Unsalted butter

subs.note: Fine in a batter or a pan. Not in anything that needs butter to be solid — pastry, creaming, or browning.

items.heartNote: 51% saturated fat. Used here only in teaspoon amounts as a finishing fat, where you can actually taste it.

items.name: Extra-firm tofu
items.tips: Press it 15 minutes under a cutting board and a heavy pot, then freeze and thaw it once for a chewier, meatier texture.

items.name: Tempeh
items.tips: Steam it 10 minutes before marinating — it removes the bitterness people blame tempeh for.

items.name: Chickpeas, canned no-salt-added

subs.note: Dry lentils need about 25 minutes of simmering and enough extra liquid to cover them.

items.tips: Drained weight of a 15 oz can is about 250 g. Save the aquafaba.

items.name: Cannellini beans, canned no-salt-added
items.tips: Blend half a can into any soup and it turns creamy with no cream at all.

items.name: Brown lentils (dry)

subs.note: Canned beans are already cooked, so add them near the end rather than at the start.

items.tips: No soaking, 25 minutes, holds its shape. One dollar feeds four people.

items.name: Red lentils (dry)
items.tips: Collapses into a creamy purée in 15 minutes — this is what makes dal thick without any dairy.

items.name: Phyllo dough
items.tips: Thaw it overnight in the fridge, never on the counter, and keep the stack under a damp towel while you work or it shatters.

items.name: Puff pastry
items.tips: Buy the all-butter kind if the store has it. It is the difference between a pastry that tastes like a bakery and one that tastes like a box.

items.name: Boneless skinless chicken thighs
items.tips: Thighs are cheaper, more forgiving, and only about 15 more calories per serving than breast.

subs.note: Add about two cups of extra liquid and 25 minutes. Brown the aromatics harder to make up the savor.

items.name: Salmon fillet
items.heartNote: AHA recommends two servings of fatty fish per week for people managing heart disease. Salmon is the easiest way to hit that.

items.name: Shrimp (raw, peeled)
items.tips: Frozen raw shrimp thaw in 10 minutes under cool water and cook in 3 — the fastest omnivore add-on there is.

items.name: Top sirloin steak, lean
items.heartNote: Red meat is the one to keep occasional when heart disease is in the picture — think a 3-4 oz portion a couple times a month, sliced thin over a vegetable-forward plate rather than a slab on its own.

items.name: Italian chicken sausage
items.heartNote: One link carries roughly 600 mg sodium. Use one link split across four servings as a flavoring, not as the protein.

items.name: Ground beef, 90% lean
items.heartNote: 90/10 carries about a third less saturated fat than 80/20 and browns just as well if you resist stirring it.

items.name: Beef chuck roast
items.tips: Chuck is the cut for a slow cooker. Its collagen turns to gelatin over hours, which is why it shreds and a lean roast just dries out.

items.name: Center-cut bacon
items.heartNote: Processed meat is the one category the evidence is least kind to. Used here the way anchovy is used — two slices seasoning a pot for six, not a plate of it.

items.name: Chicken andouille sausage
items.heartNote: One link is roughly 750 mg of sodium. In a gumbo for six that is fine; as a main course it is most of a heart-mode day.

items.name: Lump crabmeat
items.tips: Fold it, never stir it. Every extra pass breaks the lumps you paid for.

items.name: Sushi-grade ahi tuna
items.heartNote: Very lean, so it carries far less omega-3 than salmon. Eat it for the protein and the pleasure, not as your oily-fish serving.

items.name: Quinoa (dry)
items.tips: Rinse it in a fine strainer or it tastes soapy. Toast it dry for 2 minutes before adding water.

items.name: Farro (dry)
items.tips: Cook it like pasta in plenty of salted water, 25 minutes, drain. Keeps 5 days and makes any bowl feel like a restaurant grain bowl.

items.name: Old-fashioned rolled oats
items.heartNote: The beta-glucan fiber in oats is one of the few foods with an FDA-authorized heart-health claim — about 3 g a day measurably lowers LDL.

items.name: Whole wheat pasta (dry)
items.tips: If the kids resist whole wheat, start with half whole wheat and half regular in the same pot.

items.name: Corn tortillas
items.tips: Char them straight on a gas burner for 20 seconds a side. That one step is the difference between a taco and a great taco.

items.name: Whole grain bread
items.heartNote: Bread is a top-3 sodium source in the American diet, not because it is salty-tasting but because we eat so much of it. Compare labels — good loaves run 110-150 mg a slice.

items.name: Panko breadcrumbs
items.tips: Toast panko in a dry skillet with a little olive oil and lemon zest, then scatter it over pasta or roasted vegetables. It is the crunch that makes a plate feel finished.

items.name: Cornstarch
items.tips: Tossing tofu or chicken in cornstarch before searing is the restaurant trick for a shatteringly crisp exterior without deep frying.

subs.note: Cocoa is chocolate with the fat taken out — add about a tablespoon of butter or oil per ounce of chocolate replaced.
A liquid sweetener where a dry one was: take about three tablespoons of other liquid out per cup, and expect a softer bake.

items.name: Crushed tomatoes, no salt added
items.tips: San Marzano-style whole peeled tomatoes crushed by hand beat every pre-crushed can. Two minutes of work.

items.name: Tomato paste
items.tips: Fry the paste in oil for 60 seconds until it darkens before adding liquid. That is where deep flavor comes from without meat. Buy the tube so it keeps.

items.name: Light coconut milk
items.heartNote: Coconut fat is highly saturated. Light coconut milk has about a third the saturated fat of full-fat and works fine in curries; stretch it with broth.

items.name: Low-sodium vegetable broth
items.heartNote: Regular broth runs 800-900 mg sodium per cup. Low-sodium runs 100-140. Switching is one of the biggest single sodium wins in home cooking.

items.name: Capers
items.tips: Rinse them. A rinsed tablespoon adds a huge pop of flavor for well under 100 mg of sodium.

subs.note: Paste brings the same concentrated tomato but none of the chew.

items.name: Low-sodium marinara sauce
items.heartNote: Jarred sauces range from 90 to 650 mg sodium per half cup. Reading that one label changes a whole week of dinners.

items.name: Extra-virgin olive oil
items.heartNote: The PREDIMED trial found a Mediterranean diet with about 4 tablespoons of extra-virgin olive oil a day cut major cardiovascular events roughly 30% versus a low-fat diet. Olive oil is not the compromise here — it is the intervention.

items.name: Toasted sesame oil
items.tips: Finishing oil, not cooking oil. Add it off the heat or it turns bitter.

items.name: Refined coconut oil
items.heartNote: 82% saturated fat — more than butter or lard. The AHA advises against it for everyday cooking. Used here only where the flavor is the dish, in teaspoon amounts.

items.name: Avocado oil
items.tips: Smoke point around 500°F and the same monounsaturated profile as olive oil. This is the oil for a screaming-hot grill or wok, where olive oil would burn.

items.name: Dijon mustard
items.tips: A teaspoon of Dijon is what holds a vinaigrette together. It is also 55 mg of sodium — a rounding error next to bottled dressing.

items.name: Low-sodium soy sauce
items.heartNote: Even low-sodium soy sauce is about 530 mg per tablespoon. Use it as seasoning for a whole pan, not per plate, and skip the table bottle.

items.name: White miso paste
items.tips: Keeps a year in the fridge. A tablespoon whisked into a vinaigrette, a soup, or roasted vegetables adds the savory depth people think they need meat for.

subs.note: You lose the sweetness and the vinegar. A pinch of sugar and a splash of vinegar gets most of it back.

items.name: Thai red curry paste

subs.note: Powder needs frying in oil for a minute to wake up; paste does not.

items.dietNote: Many brands contain shrimp paste. Maesri and Thai Kitchen make vegetarian versions — check the label.

items.name: Tahini
items.tips: Tahini plus lemon plus water plus garlic is a sauce that goes on everything. It seizes up before it loosens — keep whisking in water.

items.name: Pure maple syrup
items.tips: Northeast Ohio is maple country — local syrup from a Geauga or Summit County sugarhouse is a genuine upgrade.

items.name: Nutritional yeast
items.tips: The vegetarian answer to parmesan: same savory hit, no saturated fat, no sodium.

items.name: Raw almonds
items.heartNote: Roughly an ounce of nuts a day is one of the most consistent findings in cardiovascular nutrition — associated with meaningfully lower coronary heart disease risk.

items.name: Walnuts
items.heartNote: The only common nut with a meaningful amount of plant omega-3 (ALA) — about 2.5 g per ounce.

items.name: Raw cashews
items.tips: Soaked and blended, cashews make a cream sauce with no dairy at all.

items.name: Ground flaxseed
items.tips: Must be ground to absorb the omega-3s, and keep it in the freezer — it goes rancid fast.

items.name: Kosher salt
items.heartNote: A teaspoon of Diamond Crystal kosher salt is about 1,100 mg sodium; table salt is nearly double that per teaspoon because the crystals pack tighter. Recipes here salt the cooking water and the dish lightly and finish with acid instead.

items.name: Smoked paprika
items.tips: Smoke without meat. This is the spice that makes vegetarian beans and lentils taste like they have bacon in them.

garden.harvest: Perennial in zone 6 — comes back stronger every year and dries beautifully

subs.note: Fresh basil goes in off the heat. Cooked, it turns gray and loses most of what you wanted from it.
Add the sprigs whole and fish them out at the end.
Fresh garlic is far milder by weight than powder — about two cloves per teaspoon. Cook it in fat for a minute or it stays raw and harsh.
Fresh onion brings water with it — give it a few minutes in the pan before the rest of the recipe carries on.

items.name: Garam masala
items.tips: Add it at the end, not the beginning — it is a finishing blend and its aroma cooks off.

items.name: Fennel seed
items.tips: Fennel seed plus smoked paprika plus red pepper flakes is what makes mushrooms or lentils taste like Italian sausage.

subs.note: Fresh ginger is mostly water, so it takes several times the weight of the ground. Grate it rather than chopping.

items.name: Ground allspice
items.tips: The backbone of Jamaican jerk. One berry tastes like cinnamon, clove and nutmeg at once, which is where the name comes from.

items.name: Ground nutmeg
items.tips: Grate it whole. Pre-ground nutmeg loses most of what makes it worth having within a few months.

items.name: Sichuan peppercorns
items.tips: Not heat — a citrusy, tingling numbness the Chinese call ma. Toast the husks in a dry pan and grind them yourself; the pre-ground kind is dust.

items.name: Brown mustard seeds
items.tips: Drop them into hot oil and wait for them to pop before anything else goes in. That thirty seconds is a whole layer of flavor.

items.name: Saffron threads

subs.note: Turmeric gives the color and none of the perfume. It is a stand-in for the look, not the taste.

garden.sow: Plant Crocus sativus corms in September
garden.harvest: Late October, one flower at a time
garden.note: Hardy to zone 6. Fifty corms give a household enough saffron for a year of paella.

items.tips: Crush the threads and steep them in a tablespoon of warm water or broth for ten minutes before they go in. Dropped in dry, most of the color and aroma stays locked in the thread.

items.name: Ground sumac

subs.note: Sumac is dried lemon, essentially. Zest plus a squeeze of juice covers it.

items.tips: Tart and purple. Sprinkled over anything beige — hummus, rice, roast cauliflower — it does the job salt would, with none of the sodium.

items.name: Berbere

subs.note: Paprika plus cayenne gets the color and heat; you lose the fenugreek and the warm spices that make berbere itself.

items.tips: Chile, fenugreek, ginger, cardamom, allspice and more, toasted and ground. It is the flavor of Ethiopian cooking, and a spoonful transforms lentils.

items.name: Old Bay seasoning
items.heartNote: Mostly celery salt — roughly 160 mg of sodium in a quarter teaspoon. Season with it, then taste before adding any other salt.

subs.note: Powdered sugar has cornstarch in it and dissolves cold. Granulated will stay gritty in an icing.

items.name: Fresh cranberries

subs.note: Dried cranberries are sweetened, so cut the sugar in the recipe by about half.

items.tips: Buy two bags in November and freeze one. They keep a year and cook straight from frozen.

items.name: Fresh sage

subs.note: A real change of flavor, not just of form. Sage is what makes brown butter taste like brown butter.

garden.harvest: Perennial in zone 6 — it comes back every spring and wants no attention

items.tips: Fry whole leaves in olive oil for 20 seconds until they go translucent and crisp. Best garnish of the autumn.

garden.harvest: August — needs heat and room to sprawl

items.name: Chipotles in adobo

subs.note: Smoked paprika carries the smoke but almost no heat.

items.tips: Freeze leftovers in tablespoon blobs on parchment. A whole can never gets used at once.

items.name: Grapefruit
items.heartNote: Grapefruit interferes with several common medications, including some statins. If anyone at the table takes one, check with a pharmacist before making it a habit.

items.name: Bread flour
items.tips: Two more grams of protein per hundred than all-purpose. That is the chew in a pizza crust and the pull in a focaccia.

items.name: Instant yeast
items.tips: Instant needs no proofing — stir it straight into the flour. Keep the jar in the freezer and it lasts years.

items.name: Molasses
items.tips: A tablespoon carries as much potassium as a banana and real iron besides. Use unsulphured; blackstrap is bitter unless the recipe asks for it.

items.name: Unsweetened applesauce
items.tips: Swapping applesauce for half the oil in a quick bread keeps it moist and cuts the fat without anyone noticing.

subs.note: The crunch is the point of chili crisp and flakes have none of it. Fry them in a spoonful of oil with a sliced garlic clove.

items.name: Arborio rice
items.tips: The starch on the outside of the grain is the sauce. Never rinse rice for risotto.

items.name: Short-grain sushi rice
items.tips: Rinse until the water runs clear — four or five changes. That is what keeps the grains distinct instead of gluey.

items.name: Basmati rice
items.tips: Soak it 20 minutes before cooking. The grains double in length instead of breaking, which is the whole point of basmati.

items.name: Stone-ground grits
items.tips: Stone-ground take 45 minutes and taste like corn. Instant take five and taste like nothing. This is a case where the slow version is worth it.

items.name: Pearl barley
items.heartNote: Barley carries the same beta-glucan soluble fiber as oats — the fiber with an FDA-authorized health claim for lowering LDL cholesterol. Cup for cup it has more fiber than almost any other grain in the store.

items.name: Bulgur wheat
items.tips: Fine bulgur needs no cooking at all — just an equal volume of boiling water and 20 minutes under a lid.

items.name: Dried chickpeas

subs.note: Only for cooked applications. Falafel needs raw soaked chickpeas and canned ones will fall apart.

items.tips: A pound costs about a dollar and yields what four cans do. Soak overnight, or in 3 hours with hot water and a teaspoon of baking soda.

items.name: Popcorn kernels
items.tips: A quarter cup of kernels makes about eight cups popped, costs about fifteen cents, and is a whole grain. Microwave bags cost ten times as much for less.

subs.note: Chili powder is a blend with cumin and oregano already in it, so go easy on those elsewhere in the recipe.
Same volume, but it will not thicken and it can split if you boil it. Take the pan off the heat before it goes in.
Soak them in boiling water for 15 minutes and blend with an equal volume of water until completely smooth.

items.name: Low-fat buttermilk

subs.note: Stir a tablespoon of vinegar or lemon juice into a cup of milk and let it sit five minutes. It curdles, which is the point.

items.tips: Its acid both tenderizes and gives baking soda something to react with. That is why buttermilk biscuits rise the way they do.

items.name: Monterey Jack
items.tips: The best melting cheese in an American grocery store — it goes liquid without breaking or turning greasy.

items.name: Swiss cheese
items.heartNote: About 190 mg sodium per 100 g — a third of what cheddar carries, and the lowest-sodium common sandwich cheese.

items.name: Halloumi
items.heartNote: Halloumi is brined, so it is salty on purpose — around 1,000 mg sodium per 100 g. Two slices a person on a platter is a garnish; a whole block is a sodium problem.

items.name: Queso fresco
items.tips: It softens but does not melt, which is exactly what you want crumbled over something hot.

subs.note: Nonfat Greek yogurt swaps one for one cold. Off the heat only — it splits if you boil it.

items.name: Oat milk
items.heartNote: Creamier than soy in coffee, but with about a quarter the protein. If oat milk is the household default, the protein has to come from somewhere else on the plate.

subs.note: Cream cheese is tangier and stiffer. Loosen it with a spoonful of cream and it stands in for mascarpone in a cold dessert.

items.name: Sourdough bread
items.tips: Stale sourdough is the best crouton, the best panzanella and the best ribollita. Do not throw the heel away.

items.name: Ladyfingers (savoiardi)
items.tips: Buy the hard Italian savoiardi, not the soft cake kind. Soft ones dissolve into paste the second they touch coffee.

items.name: Yellow mustard
items.tips: Six calories a tablespoon and real flavor. It is the cheapest way to make a lean sandwich taste like something.

items.name: Barbecue sauce
items.heartNote: A third sugar and about 175 mg sodium a tablespoon. Brushed on at the end it is a glaze; poured over it is a dessert sauce on dinner.

items.name: Louisiana-style hot sauce
items.heartNote: About 190 mg sodium a teaspoon, but nobody uses more than that. As a way to make food taste like more without more salt, it earns its shelf space.

items.name: Worcestershire sauce

subs.note: Soy sauce plus a few drops of vinegar. Standard Worcestershire contains anchovy, so this is also the vegetarian swap.

items.dietNote: Contains anchovy. Annie's and a few other brands make a vegan version.

garden.sow: Plant a root cutting in April
garden.note: Plant it where you want it forever — it comes back from any scrap of root left behind.

subs.note: You lose the heat and the acidity — add a squeeze of lemon.

items.name: Soba noodles
items.tips: Rinse cooked soba under cold water and rub the strands. Washing the surface starch off is what keeps them from gluing together.

items.name: Udon noodles
items.tips: Frozen udon is better than dried and cooks in 90 seconds from frozen.

items.name: Ramen noodles (no seasoning packet)
items.heartNote: The noodles are not the sodium problem — the seasoning packet is, at 1,500-1,800 mg. Throw it out and build the broth yourself and a bowl of ramen lands under 700.

items.name: Masa harina
items.tips: Masa is nixtamalized — cooked in lime water — which is what makes tortillas smell like tortillas and also frees the corn's niacin. Plain cornmeal cannot do it.

items.name: Rice paper wrappers
items.tips: Two seconds in warm water, no more. It should still feel stiff when it comes out — it keeps softening on the board while you fill it.

items.name: Wonton wrappers
items.tips: They freeze well. Keep the stack under plastic while you fill — a dry edge will not seal.

items.name: Full-fat coconut milk

subs.note: Light has about a third the fat. Fine in a curry; it will not whip and it will not set a dessert.

items.heartNote: About 21 g saturated fat per 100 g — the most concentrated saturated fat in the plant kingdom. Reach for the light can unless the dish genuinely needs the body.

items.name: Dried ancho chiles
items.tips: A dried poblano. Toast it 30 seconds a side until it smells like raisins and tobacco, then soak it in hot water — that is the base of every real red sauce.

items.name: Doubanjiang (fermented chili bean paste)
items.heartNote: Very salty — about 900 mg of sodium a tablespoon. One tablespoon seasons a mapo tofu for four; treat it as the salt in the dish and add none separately.
items.tips: Chop it before it goes in the pan and fry it in oil until the oil turns red. That step is what separates real mapo tofu from a brown sauce.

items.name: Chinkiang black vinegar

subs.note: Balsamic is sweeter and less smoky, but it is the closest thing in an American pantry.

items.tips: Malty, almost like balsamic's savory cousin. A teaspoon off the heat at the end wakes up any braise.

subs.note: Dry sherry is closer, dry white wine is fine. Skip the salted 'cooking wine' at the grocery store.

items.name: Vegetarian mushroom stir-fry sauce
items.tips: The vegetarian answer to oyster sauce — same glossy, slightly sweet body, built on shiitake instead.

items.name: Mirin

subs.note: Halve the amount and add a splash of rice vinegar — mirin is sweet but also acidic and much less concentrated than honey.

items.tips: Buy hon-mirin if you can find it. 'Aji-mirin' is mostly corn syrup and salt.

items.name: Red miso paste
items.tips: Aged longer than white miso and about twice as assertive. Never boil it — the aroma is the first thing to go.

items.name: Kombu (dried kelp)
items.tips: Cold-steep a piece in water overnight and you have dashi — a clear, deeply savory broth with no animal in it and almost no sodium.

items.name: Fish sauce

subs.note: Soy plus a squeeze of lime gets most of the way there for a vegetarian table. A teaspoon of white miso adds the funk back.

items.heartNote: About 1,400 mg sodium a tablespoon — the saltiest thing in most kitchens. It is a seasoning for a whole pot, and a dish using it needs no other salt.

items.name: Thai green curry paste
items.dietNote: Many brands contain shrimp paste. Maesri and Thai Kitchen make vegetarian versions — check the label.

subs.note: Lime brings the sourness but none of the raisiny depth. Add a teaspoon of brown sugar with it.
Balsamic reduced by half is the closest substitute — sweet, thick and sour in the same proportions.

items.name: Ghee

subs.note: Butter burns where ghee does not — keep the heat lower if you swap.

items.heartNote: Butterfat with the water and milk solids removed, so it is even more saturated than butter. Used here a teaspoon at a time to bloom spices, which is a job no other fat does as well.

subs.note: Italian pepper flakes are hotter and less fruity. Use half and you land in the right place.

garden.note: Peaches are marginal in zone 6a — a late frost takes the buds most years. Buy them from an orchard in August instead; that is when Ohio peaches are worth eating.

items.name: Pine nuts

subs.note: Walnuts in pesto are the traditional Ligurian thrift move, not a compromise.

items.tips: Toast them in a dry pan and do not walk away. They go from pale to burnt in about fifteen seconds.

items.name: Hazelnuts
items.tips: Roast at 350°F for 12 minutes, then rub them in a dish towel while warm — most of the bitter skin comes off.

items.name: Dried apricots
items.heartNote: More potassium per ounce than a banana, and the fiber comes along with the sugar. Still concentrated sugar — a handful, not a bowl.

shop.label: cans (14 oz) young green jackfruit in brine

items.name: Chopped clams, canned
items.heartNote: Clams are one of the densest iron sources in any grocery store — a single can carries more than a steak.

items.name: Hominy, canned
items.tips: Rinse it hard. Canned hominy comes packed in a liquid that tastes like the can.

items.name: Pumpkin puree, canned
items.tips: Buy plain pumpkin, not pumpkin pie filling. The second one is mostly sugar.

items.name: Artichoke hearts, canned
items.tips: Buy them packed in water, not oil, and squeeze them dry before they hit a hot pan.

items.name: Sauerkraut
items.tips: Buy it refrigerated, not canned — the canned kind is pasteurized, so the live cultures are gone and so is most of the snap.

items.name: Bamboo shoots, canned
items.tips: Rinse them well and blanch for a minute if they smell of the can — most of that flavor is in the packing liquid.

garden.sow: Seed or divide a clump in April
garden.note: A perennial that comes back a little bigger every year and is the first green thing out of the ground in an Ohio spring. Cut it hard; it likes it.

items.name: Napa cabbage

garden.sow: Direct sow late July for a fall crop
garden.note: Bolts in spring heat in Ohio. Grow it as a fall vegetable and it is easy.

items.tips: The white ribs and the green leaves cook at different speeds. Cut the ribs off and give them a two-minute head start.

items.name: Red cabbage

garden.sow: Transplants out mid-April or late July

items.tips: Acid keeps it magenta. Toss shredded red cabbage with vinegar or lime the moment you cut it or it turns a dull blue in the pan.

items.name: Mung bean sprouts
items.tips: They go slimy in three days. Buy them the day you need them and add them at the very end, off the heat, so they stay squeaky.

garden.note: A fall crop. Needs loose soil a foot deep to grow straight.

items.name: Poblano pepper
items.tips: Char the skin black over a flame or under the broiler, steam it covered ten minutes, and it slips off. That step is the whole flavor.

items.name: Serrano pepper
items.tips: Roughly twice the heat of a jalapeno and thinner-walled, so it disappears into a salsa instead of sitting in it.

items.name: Tomatillos

garden.note: Plant two — they will not set fruit alone.

items.tips: Peel the husk and wash the sticky film off, or the salsa tastes soapy.

items.name: Thai bird chiles

garden.sow: Start indoors in March, out after Memorial Day

items.tips: Freeze the bag whole. They grate straight from frozen and lose nothing.

items.name: Plantains
items.tips: Green is a starchy vegetable, black is a dessert. For sweet fried plantains wait until the skin is more black than yellow — nobody waits long enough.

items.name: Mango
items.tips: Cut down either side of the flat pit, score the halves in a grid, then push the skin inside out.

items.name: Pineapple
items.tips: It is ripe when a leaf near the center pulls out with almost no effort and the base smells like pineapple.

garden.note: Ready when the stem slips off the fruit with thumb pressure.

items.name: Sweet cherries
items.tips: Frozen dark sweet cherries are picked ripe and cost a third as much in February. For anything cooked they are the better buy.

garden.harvest: July, and again in September for everbearing types
garden.note: Heritage and Caroline are the reliable everbearers for northern Ohio.

garden.sow: Direct sow every two weeks, April and September
garden.note: The fastest thing in the garden and the best crop to hand a child.
Frost converts their starch to sugar. Parsnips pulled in November taste nothing like September ones.
Sweeter after a freeze. Picks all winter under a row cover in zone 6a.

items.name: Okra

garden.sow: Direct sow in June once soil is warm
garden.note: Pick pods at three inches. A day later they are wood.

items.tips: Slime is water plus low heat. High dry heat — a hot grill, a hot roast, a hot skillet — or a hit of acid keeps it firm.

items.name: Lemongrass

garden.sow: Root a grocery stalk in water, pot it in May
garden.note: Overwinters indoors on a sunny sill.

items.tips: Only the bottom four inches are tender. Bruise the stalk with the back of a knife before slicing to wake up the oils.

items.name: Spaghetti squash

garden.note: Cures on the counter and keeps until February.

items.tips: Cut it into rings across the equator, not lengthwise. The strands run around the fruit, so rings give you long strands instead of short ones.

garden.note: Never eat the leaves — they carry enough oxalic acid to make you sick. Stop picking by July so the crown rebuilds.

items.name: Butter lettuce

garden.sow: Direct sow April and again in September

items.tips: The cupped inner leaves are the sturdiest lettuce wrap there is.

items.name: Jicama
items.tips: Peel it like a potato, cut it into sticks, and hit it with lime and chili. It stays crisp in the fridge for a week, which is more than can be said for cut apple.

garden.note: Sweet onions bruise easily and do not store. Eat them by October.

items.name: Oyster mushrooms

garden.sow: Inoculated logs or a countertop kit, any month

items.tips: Torn into strips, dredged and fried, they are the closest thing to fried oysters or fried chicken that grows on a log.

items.name: Lower-sodium deli ham
items.heartNote: Even the lower-sodium versions run over 1,000 mg per 100 g. Two thin slices on a sandwich, not four.
